data.title: Technical Debt
data.tagline: A usable implementation choice that leaves structural issues adding to later change work
data.learningOutcome: You can recognize a maintenance burden from repeated edits and missed changes, then decide whether to address it based on impact.
data.description: When five pages each keep a copy of the login-button style, changing its color means editing five places; missing one leaves the pages inconsistent. This duplication makes later edits easier to miss. After moving the style into one shared component, you still need to check every page. Technical debt describes a maintenance burden to weigh; it does not mean every duplicate must be rewritten now or will inevitably cost more over time.

learning.assumes: You have seen duplicated code with wide change impact, or AI suggesting a later refactor.
learning.outcome: You can recognize a maintenance burden from repeated edits and missed changes, then decide whether to address it based on impact.

distinctions.label: Bug
distinctions.explanation: A bug is incorrect behavior to fix; technical debt is a maintenance burden that can exist even while the feature works.

distinctions.label: Refactoring
distinctions.explanation: Refactoring is the act of paying off debt; technical debt is the debt itself. Recording debt and paying it are two things.

explanation.title: Before: five files keep separate copies
explanation.text: Changing the button color means finding five definitions; miss Docs and its button stays gray.

explanation.title: The change: a shared component
explanation.text: Following the project's existing structure, put the button style in one shared component and let all five pages use it.

explanation.title: Feedback and boundary
explanation.text: Reopen all five pages and confirm the buttons are blue without changing other page behavior. Whether to consolidate more depends on the actual maintenance burden; not every repeated line needs rewriting.

data.boundary: Not every repeated line needs consolidation. When a color update has already missed one page and still means finding five sources, the maintenance burden is visible. Before sharing an implementation, check whether any page needs its own style.

lessonPractice.title: Five button styles were changed to blue, but four pages are blue while Docs is still gray. What does this miss show?

options.label: There are five independent definitions; the same change must be applied at each source, so one can be missed
options.feedback: Correct. Five separate sources mean the same style change must be synchronized in several places; checking the pages exposed one stale value.

options.label: The button has one shared source, but Docs is still showing a cached page
options.feedback: The example has five independent definitions; browser cache does not explain why those copies need separate edits.

options.label: The gray Docs button is an intentional permission state, so ignore the change record
options.feedback: The example gives no evidence for a permission or design difference; Docs missed the explicitly requested color change.

data.agentPrompt: In this example, the same login-button style is repeated on five pages and Docs was missed. Follow the project's existing structure to move it into a shared component, then check each page for blue buttons and unexpected changes. Tell me where to edit the style next time.
